instruction: Take each email from the Bills folder in Thunderbird, save it as a .eml file with the email subject as the filename, then move these files to the Google Drive emails folder.

path_list: Amazon Web Services Invoice Available [Account: 0123456789ab] [Invoice ID: 0123456789].eml

metadata.explanation: Task requires saving Bills folder emails as .eml files and uploading to Google Drive. Evaluator checks that 2 files exist and contain essential email headers (Subject and From) to validate they are proper email files.

llm_judge_reasons: Parameter handling is CORRECT: Lines 36-38 properly access expected.get() directly without wrapping in expected.get('rules'). The metric correctly receives the rules dictionary as the expected parameter.

OVERLY STRICT subject-to-filename matching (lines 86-93): Uses exact string comparison (subject_line != expected_subject) which will fail for minor formatting differences, encoding variations, or special character handling between email headers and filenames. Real .eml files may have Subject headers formatted differently than filenames.

HARDCODED ASSUMPTIONS about sender addresses (lines 97-100): The metric assumes specific sender emails (no-reply@amazon.com, info@x.com) without analyzing actual Bills folder data. These hardcoded values are assumptions that may not match the actual emails in the Thunderbird Bills folder.

VERIFICATION LOGIC TOO FRAGILE: The combination of exact string matching for subjects and hardcoded sender verification creates a brittle evaluator that may produce false negatives when the task is actually completed correctly but with minor variations in email formatting.

CORRECT in principle: The evaluator checks the right aspects (file count, email headers present, content matching), but the implementation is too strict for real-world email file handling where formatting variations are normal.
llm_judge_fix_suggestions: Use fuzzy/normalized string matching for subject comparison: Strip special characters, normalize whitespace, and use case-insensitive comparison. Email subjects in .eml files may be encoded differently than filenames.

Remove hardcoded sender assumptions: Either extract expected senders from actual Bills folder data during task generation, or use more flexible sender validation (e.g., check domain matches like '@amazon.com' instead of exact address).

Add tolerance for email header variations: .eml files can have different encodings (quoted-printable, base64) and formatting. Consider using email parsing libraries (email.parser) instead of simple string matching.

Consider relaxing to warning-level checks: If exact matching is desired, make it a partial credit deduction rather than complete failure, or provide clear documentation that exact formatting is required.
